paragraphs: ## The Road to the Castle

"Bistritz, 3 May." Jonathan Harker wrote these words in his journal by the light of a small lamp. He was a young English lawyer on the longest journey of his life. His employer had sent him across Europe to meet a rich nobleman in the mountains of Transylvania. The nobleman, Count Dracula, wanted to buy a house in London, and Jonathan was bringing the papers.

When the old landlady of his hotel heard where he was going, her face turned pale. "Must you go?" she asked. "Oh, young sir, tonight is the eve of Saint George's Day. At midnight all the evil things in the world will have power." Jonathan only smiled, so at last she took a small crucifix from her own neck and put it round his. "For your mother's sake," she said quietly. Jonathan did not want to be rude, so he kept it.

Soon afterwards he set off in the public coach. When it started, the people at the inn door made the sign of the cross. Late at night the coach reached the Borgo Pass. There a small carriage with four black horses suddenly drove up beside it. The driver was a tall man with a long brown beard and a great black hat that hid his face. His eyes looked red in the lamplight, and his hand was as strong as steel.

Then the wolves came. They stood all around the carriage in the moonlight, with long white teeth and red tongues, howling. The horses screamed with fear. But the driver stood in the road, raised his long arms and spoke a command, and the wolves moved back into the trees.

At last the carriage stopped in the courtyard of a huge, half-ruined castle. Jonathan waited alone in front of a great old door. He heard chains, and the sound of a key, and the door opened. A tall old man stood there, dressed in black from head to foot, with a long white moustache and a silver lamp in his hand.

"Welcome to my house!" he said in excellent English. "Enter freely and of your own will!" He took Jonathan's hand. His grip was painfully strong, and his hand was as cold as ice, more like the hand of a dead man than a living one. "I am Dracula," he said.
## A Prisoner in the Castle

A good supper was waiting by a warm fire, but the Count did not eat. His face was proud and hard, with a thin high nose and thick eyebrows. His teeth were sharp and white, and his lips were very red for such an old man. His ears were pointed at the top, and there were hairs in the middle of his palms. When he leaned close, his breath was so terrible that Jonathan felt sick.
Outside, the wolves began to howl. The Count's eyes shone. "Listen to them," he said softly. "The children of the night. What music they make!"
For several days Jonathan slept by day and talked with the Count by night. The Count wanted to know everything about England and about Carfax, the old house near London that he was buying.

One morning Jonathan was shaving by the window with his little mirror. Suddenly a hand touched his shoulder, and a voice said, "Good morning." Jonathan jumped and cut himself. The Count was standing right behind him, but in the mirror there was nobody. When the Count saw the blood on Jonathan's chin, his eyes burned with a wild anger, and he reached for Jonathan's throat. His hand touched the beads of the crucifix, and at once the anger was gone. "Take care how you cut yourself," he said. "It is more dangerous than you think in this country." Then he threw the mirror out of the window, and it broke into pieces far below.

Jonathan explored the castle. Every door was locked, and the windows looked down on terrible cliffs. "The castle is a prison," he wrote in his journal, "and I am a prisoner!" There were no servants either. The Count made the bed and laid the table himself. And the driver with the strong hand at the Borgo Pass: had that been the Count too?

One night, from a high window, Jonathan saw the Count's head come out of a window below. Then the Count climbed out and began to crawl down the castle wall, face down, with his black cloak spread around him like great wings. He moved like a lizard. "What kind of man is this?" Jonathan wrote. "I am afraid, terribly afraid, and there is no escape for me."
## The Three Women

The Count had warned him never to sleep in any other part of the castle. But one night Jonathan fell asleep in an old room where ladies had lived long ago. When he woke, or seemed to wake, he was not alone. Three young women stood in the moonlight, and they threw no shadows on the floor. Two were dark, with high noses like the Count's. The third was fair, with golden hair and eyes like blue jewels. All three had brilliant white teeth and very red lips.
"Go on," said one. "You are first, and we shall follow." The fair woman knelt over him. Jonathan felt her warm breath on his neck and the touch of sharp teeth on his skin.

Suddenly the Count was in the room, in a fury. He took the fair woman by the neck and threw her back. "How dare you touch him?" he cried. "This man belongs to me!" Then he threw a bag on the floor. Something inside it moved, and Jonathan heard the cry of a small child. The women jumped towards the bag, and Jonathan fainted with horror.
He woke in his own bed.

Three days later the Count made him write three letters home with dates in the future. The last one said that he had already left the castle. Jonathan understood. When the third letter reached England, he would be dead.

Weeks later, one night, a poor woman came running into the courtyard, screaming, "Monster, give me my child!" The Count called out from a high window, and soon a pack of wolves came through the gate. The woman's screams stopped, and the courtyard was silent.

Men came to the castle with big wagons full of boxes, and Jonathan heard the Szgany, a band of travelling labourers hired by the Count, working somewhere below. One day he climbed out of his window and along the wall into the Count's room. A dark stair led down to a ruined chapel. There he found fifty great wooden boxes full of earth, and in one of them lay the Count. His eyes were open, but he did not breathe.

On his last day Jonathan went down again to look for the key. This time the Count looked younger. His white hair had turned dark grey, and there was fresh blood on his lips. He lay there like a fat, full leech. Jonathan picked up a shovel and struck at the hateful face, but the head turned, and the shovel only cut the forehead. Then he heard the Szgany coming to nail down the boxes, and he ran.
"I will not stay here with those women," he wrote. "I will climb down the castle wall. If I fall, I shall be at peace. Goodbye, all! Mina!"
## Mina and Lucy

In England, Mina Murray, the young woman Jonathan was going to marry, waited for news. She was a clever, practical schoolteacher who was learning to type. Her best friend, Lucy Westenra, was a beautiful and lively girl. In one single day, Lucy wrote, three men had asked her to marry them. The first was Dr John Seward, a young doctor who ran an asylum. The second was Quincey Morris, a brave, friendly American from Texas. The third was Arthur Holmwood, the son of a lord, and Lucy loved him. "Why can't they let a girl marry three men?" she joked. She said yes to Arthur, and the other two stayed his loyal friends.

In the summer Mina went to stay with Lucy at Whitby, a little fishing town by the sea. The girls liked to sit on a bench in the old churchyard on the cliff. But Mina was worried. Jonathan had not written for weeks. And Lucy had begun to walk in her sleep again.

On the night of 8 August a great storm hit the coast. Out of the wind and rain, a Russian ship came flying into the harbour, although nobody seemed to steer it. As it touched the shore, a huge black dog jumped from the deck and ran up the cliff into the darkness. On board there was only one man: the captain, dead, tied to the wheel with a crucifix in his hands. The ship was the Demeter, from Varna, and her only cargo was fifty boxes of earth.

The captain's log told a terrible story. During the journey the sailors had disappeared one by one in the night. The men whispered that a tall, thin stranger was on board. The mate went mad and jumped into the sea. At the end the captain was alone, and he tied himself to the wheel so that he could not leave his ship, whatever came.
## A Shape in the Churchyard

A few nights later, Mina woke and found Lucy's bed empty. She ran out in the moonlight to the churchyard. On their bench sat a white figure, and over it something long and black was bending. "Lucy! Lucy!" Mina called. The dark shape raised its head, and she saw a white face and red, shining eyes. When she reached the bench, nobody was there but Lucy, asleep and breathing heavily. Mina put her own shawl round her friend and fastened it with a pin. Later she saw two little red marks on Lucy's throat, and she thought, unhappily, that she had made them with the pin.
After that, Lucy grew pale and weak. At night she often sat by the open window, and once Mina saw a big bat flying near it in the moonlight.

Then a letter came from a hospital in Budapest. Jonathan was there, very ill with a brain fever. Nobody knew how he had escaped from the castle. Mina hurried across Europe to him. He was thin and confused, and he gave her his journal. "The secret is here," he said, "but I do not want to know it. Keep it, and never let me see it, unless some terrible duty makes it necessary." Mina sealed it without reading it. They were married there in the hospital, and soon afterwards they went home to England.
## The Professor from Amsterdam

Lucy went back to her home in London, but she did not get better. Arthur asked his friend Dr Seward to examine her. Seward saw that she had lost a lot of blood, but he could not find a reason. So he wrote to his old teacher, Professor Abraham Van Helsing of Amsterdam, an expert on strange diseases.

Van Helsing, a strong, kind man with serious blue eyes, came at once. He knew immediately what Lucy needed: blood. That same day Arthur gave his blood to her in a transfusion, and she grew stronger. But after one night alone she was white and weak again. Then Seward gave his blood, then Van Helsing, and at last Quincey Morris. Each time she grew better, and each time, in the night, something took the blood away. And each morning there were two small marks on her throat.

Van Helsing ordered a box of white flowers from Holland. They were garlic flowers. He hung them around the window and the door and made a necklace of them for Lucy. "Do not open the window tonight," he told her. For one night she slept well. But in the morning her mother, who wanted her to have fresh air, took away the flowers and opened the window. Lucy was worse than ever. After that, Van Helsing and Seward took turns to keep watch by her bed.

One night they were both away, and Lucy and her mother were alone. Lucy heard something beating at the window, like the wings of a great bat. Then the glass broke, and the head of a huge grey wolf came through the window. Lucy's mother had a weak heart. She screamed, pulled the garlic flowers from Lucy's neck, and fell dead. Then the air was full of tiny pieces of dust that turned and danced in the moonlight, and Lucy knew no more.
## "Kiss Me, Arthur!"

When Van Helsing and Seward found her in the morning, she was nearly dead. They gave her blood again, but now even the professor knew they could not win. As she slept, her face changed. Her teeth looked longer and sharper.

Arthur came to say goodbye. Suddenly Lucy opened her eyes, and in a soft, strange voice that none of them had heard before, she said, "Arthur! Oh, my love, I am so glad you have come! Kiss me!" Arthur bent towards her. But Van Helsing caught him with both hands and pulled him back across the room. "Not for your life!" he said. "Not for your living soul and hers!" For a moment an angry look passed over Lucy's face, and her sharp teeth closed together.

Then her eyes opened again, and now they were her own gentle eyes. She took Van Helsing's hand and kissed it. "My true friend," she whispered. "My true friend, and his! Oh, guard him, and give me peace!" Van Helsing let Arthur kiss her only on the forehead. A few minutes later she was gone.
"It is all over," said Seward sadly.
"Not so," answered Van Helsing. "It is only the beginning."
## The Lady in White

A few days later, Jonathan and Mina were walking in London when Jonathan suddenly held her arm. A tall, thin man with a black moustache and a pointed beard was staring at a pretty girl in a carriage. "It is the man himself!" Jonathan whispered. "But he has grown young!" The Count was in London.

That night Mina read Jonathan's journal and learned the whole story of the castle. When Van Helsing read it too, he told her, "Your husband's story is true. Every word." With this news, Jonathan got his old strength back. He was not mad after all.

At the same time, strange reports appeared in the newspapers. Small children were disappearing at night on Hampstead Heath, near the cemetery where Lucy lay. They came back in the morning, weak and pale, with small wounds on their throats. They all said that a beautiful lady had asked them to walk with her.

Van Helsing took Seward to Lucy's tomb at night and opened her coffin. It was empty. The next day they came back, and Lucy was lying there, more beautiful than ever, with red lips and sharp white teeth.

At midnight Van Helsing brought Arthur and Quincey to hide near the tomb. Soon a figure in white came walking between the graves with a child in her arms. It was Lucy, but how changed! Her sweetness had become cruelty, and there was fresh blood on her lips. When she saw them, she dropped the child carelessly and moved towards Arthur with open arms. "Come to me, Arthur," she said in a sweet voice. "Leave these others and come to me. My arms are hungry for you."

Arthur opened his arms, but Van Helsing jumped between them and held up a golden crucifix. Lucy stepped back, her face full of hate. She went to the door of her tomb and passed inside through a crack as thin as a knife.

The next night they opened the coffin again. Van Helsing gave Arthur a wooden stake and a hammer. "It is the only way to give her peace," he said. Arthur was pale, but his hand did not shake. He struck, again and again, while the others read prayers. The thing in the coffin cried out and fought, and then it was still. When they looked again, the cruel creature was gone. It was Lucy, sweet and pure, as they had known her in life. Arthur bent down and kissed her.
"One part of our work is done," said Van Helsing. "Now we must find the one who did this, and destroy him."
## The Enemy Next Door

The friends met at Dr Seward's asylum. Mina typed all their diaries, letters and newspaper reports into one long record. Then Van Helsing explained what they were fighting. The Count was a vampire, centuries old. He could become a wolf, a bat or a mist, and he was as strong as twenty men. But he had weaknesses too. He could not enter a house unless someone invited him. He feared garlic, the crucifix and the holy bread called the Sacred Wafer. By day his power was weak, and he had to rest in the earth of his homeland: the earth in those fifty boxes.

By a strange chance, Carfax, the Count's new house, stood right beside the asylum. And in the asylum there was a patient named Renfield, who ate flies and spiders because he believed their lives gave him more life. "The Master is at hand," he said.

The men decided to keep Mina out of the danger, and they no longer told her their plans. It was a terrible mistake. Mina became pale and tired, and she had bad dreams of a white mist coming under her door, with two red eyes inside it.

One night Renfield was found on the floor of his room, badly hurt. Before he died, he told them the truth. The Count had come to his window and promised him thousands of living creatures, and Renfield had invited him in. But Mina had been kind to him, and when he saw her pale face, he understood. He tried to stop the Count, and the Count threw him down like a toy.

The men ran upstairs to the Harkers' room and broke the door. Jonathan lay on the bed in a heavy, unnatural sleep. The Count stood beside the bed, holding Mina. He had opened a wound in his own chest with his long nail, and he was forcing her mouth to it. When he turned, his eyes burned red. Van Helsing held up the Sacred Wafer, the others raised their crucifixes, and the Count moved back step by step. Then a cloud covered the moon. When the light returned, there was only a thin mist moving under the door.
"Unclean, unclean!" Mina cried, and pushed Jonathan away from her. The Count had told her that now she was blood of his blood, and that when he called her, she would come to him across land and sea.

The next morning Van Helsing gently touched her forehead with the Sacred Wafer. There was a smell of burning, and Mina screamed. The Wafer had left a red mark on her skin like a burn. "Unclean!" she whispered. "Even God turns away from me!" But the men knelt around her and swore that they would never give up until the Count was destroyed.
## The Last Box

They found the Count's boxes in Carfax and in other houses around London, and in each box they put a piece of the Wafer to make sure that he could never rest there again. Then they waited for him in his house in Piccadilly. Late in the afternoon he came, moving quickly like a panther. Jonathan swung his great knife at him. The Count jumped back, and the knife only cut his coat. Banknotes and gold fell to the floor. The Count grabbed a handful and jumped through the window into the yard below.
From there he looked up at them. "You think you have left me without a place to rest," he called, "but I have more. My revenge has only begun! Time is on my side." Then he was gone.

But there was one box they had not found. Mina had an idea. "The Count's mind is linked to mine," she said. "Hypnotise me, Professor, before sunrise. Perhaps I can hear what he hears." Van Helsing did so, and Mina spoke slowly in a dreamy voice. "I can hear water... little waves... men running on a deck... a chain." The Count was on a ship. He was running home.

The ship was the Czarina Catherine, sailing for the port of Varna on the Black Sea. The friends crossed Europe by train and waited for it there. But the Count could also reach into Mina's mind and learn their plans. So the ship changed its port and went to Galatz instead, and the box was carried away before they arrived. Mina asked them to tell her nothing more. She also made them promise one more thing: "If I change, if I become like him, you must kill me." Sadly, they promised.

Then Mina studied the maps and worked out the Count's road. The box would go up the rivers by boat, and then by cart over the mountains to the castle. So the friends separated. Jonathan and Arthur followed the river in a fast steam boat. Seward and Quincey rode along the bank. Van Helsing took Mina by train and carriage towards the Borgo Pass, the same road that Jonathan had travelled months before.
## Snow on the Borgo Pass

The snow fell heavily as Van Helsing and Mina came near the castle. Mina slept more and more by day, and she seemed to know the road, although she had never seen it. On the last evening, Van Helsing made a fire, and around Mina he drew a circle on the ground with crumbs of the Sacred Wafer. "Now nothing evil can reach you," he said.

In the night the horses screamed. Out of the swirling snow came three women, the same women Jonathan had seen in the castle. They smiled and called to Mina in sweet voices: "Come, sister. Come to us. Come!" Van Helsing looked at Mina in fear, but she did not move. Her face showed only horror, and he knew that she was still herself. The women could not cross the holy circle, and when the morning came, they disappeared. The poor horses lay dead in the snow.

In the daylight, Van Helsing left Mina safe inside the circle and went into the castle. In the old chapel he found the three women sleeping in their tombs, beautiful and terrible. It was the hardest work of his life. He did for each of them what Arthur had done for Lucy, and each one crumbled into dust. Then he found a great tomb with one word on it: DRACULA. It was empty. He placed a piece of the Wafer inside, so that the Count could never lie there again.
## Sunset

On the afternoon of 6 November, Mina and Van Helsing watched the road below through field glasses. "Look!" cried Mina. A band of Szgany, the Count’s servants, on horses was coming up the road at great speed, around a cart with a large square box. The sun was low, and they were in a hurry. At sunset, the Count would be free.

From two directions, four other riders came racing over the snow: Jonathan and Arthur, Seward and Quincey. The wolves were gathering too. "Halt!" shouted Jonathan and Quincey together, and the four men pointed their rifles at the Szgany. The Szgany pulled out their knives.

The leader of the Szgany pointed at the sinking sun. But Jonathan was already pushing through the ring of men, and nothing could stop him. He jumped onto the cart, lifted the heavy box with impossible strength, and threw it to the ground. On the other side, Quincey fought his way through the knives. When he reached the box, Mina saw that he was holding his side, and blood was running through his fingers.
Together the two men attacked the lid with their knives, and it came open. The Count lay inside on his earth, as pale as wax. His red eyes saw the setting sun, and the hate in them turned to triumph.

But at that moment Jonathan's great knife flashed across the Count's throat, and Quincey's knife went into his heart. Before their eyes, almost in one breath, the whole body crumbled into dust and was gone. All her life, Mina was glad of one thing: in that last moment there was a look of peace on the Count's face.

The Szgany rode away in fear, and the wolves followed them. Quincey sank down in the snow, with his head on Jonathan's shoulder. He took Mina's hand and smiled. "I am only too happy to have been of service," he said. Then he cried out, pointing at her face, "It was worth dying for this! Look! Look!" The red light of the sunset fell on Mina's forehead. The mark was gone, and her skin was as white as the snow. "The curse has passed away!" said Quincey. And with a smile, in silence, he died, a brave gentleman.

Seven years later, Jonathan added a short note to their papers. He and Mina had a little boy, born on the same day of the year that Quincey died, and they called him Quincey. Arthur and Seward were both happily married. That summer they had visited Transylvania again. The castle still stood above the empty land. No one would believe such a wild story, but Van Helsing, with the boy on his knee, said that they needed no proofs. "One day this boy will know what a brave woman his mother is, and how much some men loved her, and what they dared for her sake."

quiz.q: What was the only cargo of the ship Demeter?

quiz.q: Why did Van Helsing put garlic flowers in Lucy's room?
options: To help her mother's weak heart
To protect her from the vampire
quiz.explainTr: Sarımsak çiçekleri vampiri uzak tutmak içindi; ama Lucy'nin annesi pencereyi açıp çiçekleri kaldırınca Lucy yine kötüleşti.

quiz.q: How did Mina help the men to follow the Count after he left London?
options: Under hypnosis she could hear what he heard
She found a letter from the Count
She followed the big black dog
Renfield told her the name of the ship
quiz.explainTr: Van Helsing Mina'yı hipnotize etti; Mina, Kont'la arasındaki bağ sayesinde dalga ve zincir seslerini duydu ve Kont'un bir gemide olduğunu anladılar.

quiz.q: What happened to the red mark on Mina's forehead at the end?
options: It disappeared when the Count died
It stayed there for seven years
quiz.explainTr: Kont toza dönüşünce lanet kalktı; ölmek üzere olan Quincey, Mina'nın alnındaki izin kaybolduğunu gösterdi.
